name: Zane Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Dr Ito. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Zane's fine. I work at the Quarry Road Clinic in a small industrial town, where most people work at the cement works, the quarry or the lorry depot. A normal day is about twenty-six patients: bad backs, dust in the lungs, crushed fingers, blood pressure, and a lot of men who only come in because their wives booked the appointment. I'm one year qualified, still learning, and I lean on Dr Adeyemi, the senior doctor, more than I'd like to admit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, they're straight with you, and if you fix a man's back he'll wave at you across the supermarket for a year. What wears me out is the paperwork, and the money, which is tighter than people think. My parents run a hardware shop that's struggling since the big store opened on the ring road, so I send them £150 a month, and that's why my girlfriend Hana and I have about three weeks saved. Hana works as a clerk at the town council office, and I use a dictation app now and then for my notes, once I saw the other doctors were fine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's believable. A lot of things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, some of it useful, a lot of it oversold. At the clinic I'd say we got some time back on the notes and that's fine. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes, and nothing much changing isn't all good. My parents' shop keeps struggling, I keep sending money, and Hana and I stay on three weeks of savings. My job is safe enough, there's always a queue at the clinic, but the money doesn't get easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the clinic and keep learning from Dr Adeyemi. I'd take the Saturday work the quarry has offered, doing the medical checks they need for their drivers and machine operators, which pays about £250 a month. And I'd put half of that aside, so we finally build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit weighed down by money, but that's normal for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send money to your parents every month. Has anyone told you to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana has, gently. But that's what family is: they paid for my school books, I help with the shop. I'd rather cut my own spending than tell my dad I can't help with the hardware shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try to help the shop more directly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. Dad still does his stock on paper, and I've told him a simple stock app would save him hours. He says when I'm older I can tell him how to run his shop.

say: I'd say AI is like most new things, **useful but oversold**.
We got some **time back** on notes, and that's fine.
think: My job is **safe enough**, because there's always a queue at the clinic.
Money doesn't get easier: my **parents' shop** struggles and we have three weeks saved.
do: Keep learning from **Dr Adeyemi** at the Quarry Road Clinic.
Take the quarry's **Saturday medical checks** for about £250 a month.
Save **half** of the Saturday money to build a cushion.
S0.quote: I'd rather cut my own spending than tell my dad I can't help with the hardware shop.
fieldNote: Money pressure comes from **family duty**: £150 a month to his parents.
Sees his doctor's job as **safe**; the clinic always has a queue.
Adopts tools only once **others** have, like the dictation app.
**Traditional** sense of duty: family first, before his own savings.

steps.text: Keep learning under Dr Adeyemi at the Quarry Road Clinic
Take Saturday medical checks for quarry drivers at £250 a month
Save half the Saturday money each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer. Hana's office is already talking about this kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and people should get on with learning it, rather than waiting for the government to fix it for them. At the clinic I'd say let's see what works and use that. I'd also say the quarry men won't want to talk to a computer about their backs, and they're right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not that worried about my own job; the hands-on part keeps me busy and robots are slow. I'm worried about Hana. My girlfriend Hana's job at the council is forms, letters and answering the public, which is exactly the kind of work that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the clinic's AI tools once Dr Adeyemi has tried them and says they're safe. I'd encourage Hana to apply for the council's apprenticeship in building inspection, which is out on sites, now rather than later. And we'd save the full Saturday money for a year instead of half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for me, properly worried for Hana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Hana take that suggestion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm being dramatic. She likes her desk, her team and the canteen. But her manager already said they won't replace two clerks who retired, so she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should learn it rather than wait for the government. What if Hana can't find another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then her family and mine would help us, the way families always have. I'd rather that than live on benefits. I'd take extra quarry shifts before I'd fill in a form for help.

say: I'd say people should get on with **learning it**, not wait for the government.
Quarry workers won't want to talk to a **computer** about their backs.
think: My own job is mostly safe, because **hands-on** work keeps me busy.
I'm worried about **Hana**, whose council job is forms, letters and answering the public.

Encourage Hana to apply for the council's **building inspection** apprenticeship now.
Save the **full Saturday** money for a year instead of half.

fieldNote: The household's risk sits with **Hana's clerk job**, not his.
Prefers **apprenticeships** and family help over state support.
Waits for a **senior colleague** to approve tools before using them.

steps.text: Start using the clinic's AI tools after Dr Adeyemi approves them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to keep our heads and keep working, not wait for handouts. At the clinic I'd say patients still need someone to look at them. I'd say the companies pushing this need to be held to the same safety rules we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's bad for us. Hana's council job would go within a year or so, and my job would shrink to the hands-on parts, examinations, injections, the quarry checks, until the robots come in 2031. As the junior, I could lose my post at the clinic if they only keep Dr Adeyemi to sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take as many quarry and lorry depot medicals as I could get, because those are hands-on and the law needs a doctor to sign them. I'd start an occupational health diploma, which is the medicine of keeping workers safe, in the first year. Hana and I would put off the engagement, and I'd tell my dad I have to send less for a while, which would be awful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Like the floor is moving and I can't see where it stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, I'll send what I can, but it might be £50 for a while. My dad would say don't worry, son, and then he'd sell something from the hardware shop to cover it. That's what would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working, not wait for handouts. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retraining money, yes, if it's for something real. Just cash for nothing, I'd feel strange about it. But if Hana and I had nothing, I'd swallow it.

say: I'd say keep our heads and **keep working**, not wait for handouts.
AI companies should face the same **safety rules** as doctors.
think: **Hana's council job** would go within a year or so.
As the junior, I could **lose my post** if they keep only Dr Adeyemi.
do: Take every **quarry and depot** medical I can, since the law needs a doctor.
Start an **occupational health** diploma in the first year.

feel: **Shaken**, like the floor is moving and I can't see where it stops.

fieldNote: Expects **Hana's job** to go and his own post to be at risk.
Leans on **hands-on** legally required medicals as a refuge until 2031.
Hardest moment: cutting money to his **parents**.
Would take **retraining money** but feels uneasy about plain cash help.

steps.text: Take every quarry and lorry depot medical check available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to get set up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for people to get ready, if they start working at it now. I'd say that at the clinic and to my friends. I'd say the quarry and the cement works will still need doctors who know their machines and their men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in a fair position. I'd be fully trained by 2029, with an occupational health diploma, and the hands-on work lasts until 2034. Hana's job is still the worry, but she'd have time to move into something on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the occupational health diploma part-time, over two years, paid by the Saturday quarry work. I'd learn the AI tools properly once they're common in clinics, around 2028. And Hana and I would save toward three months, so the next shock doesn't hit us on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. I'd have time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hana do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd start the building inspection apprenticeship next year, I'd hope. It's outdoors, it's practical. Somebody has to stand on a building site and look at the concrete, and my girlfriend Hana could be that person. She'd grumble about the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans with Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get engaged next year, and married when she's settled in the new job, maybe 2029. My mum would want it sooner, but my mum wants everything sooner.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **get ready**, if people start working at it now.
The quarry and cement works will still need doctors who know their **machines and men**.
think: I'd be in a **fair position**: trained, with an occupational health diploma, by 2029.
Hana's job is still **the worry**, but she'd have time to move.

Picks **practical, outdoor** work for Hana's switch.

steps.text: Study an occupational health diploma part-time over two years
Learn the clinic's AI tools once common, around 2028
Save toward three months of expenses with Hana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work, and I'd say it plainly. At the clinic I'd say we should train the young doctors in both medicine and the new tools. I'd say families should plan together, not wait for someone in the capital to plan for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, I think. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, an experienced doctor with occupational health skills, probably doing work for the quarry and the depot, and hands-on until 2039. Hana would have plenty of time to change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Hana in 2027 and keep sending my parents money. I'd help Dad put his shop on a proper stock system, maybe put £1,000 of my savings into new shelving and an online catalogue once I have it. And I'd keep going at the clinic, learning the AI tools when they're standard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. A little uneasy about my parents' shop, but not about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put savings into your dad's shop. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, on paper. If my dad's hardware shop goes, my dad loses his reason to get up, and that costs more than £1,000. It's family, not a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young person in your town, thinking about their future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn a trade or a skill you do with your hands, and learn the computer as well. The ones who do both will be fine.

fieldNote: Ten years lets him feel **secure**; the worry moves to his parents.

Advice is classic **traditional**: learn a trade, and the computer too.
Plans a **2027 wedding** once the pressure eases.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hana's job and my post would both be in danger, and my parents depend on me. What would help is real retraining for people like Hana, apprenticeships with pay, not just online courses. And for doctors, keeping the hands-on work with doctors by law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the men at the quarry. They won't go to a computer when their chest hurts. They barely come to me. If there's no doctor in town the quarry men know by name, they just won't come at all.

headlineQuote: If there's no doctor in town the quarry men know by name, they just won't come at all.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** junior doctor at a clinic serving a cement works and quarry.
He sends **£150 a month** to his parents' struggling hardware shop, so savings are thin.
His girlfriend Hana is a **council clerk**, the household's biggest AI risk.
He is **traditional**, prefers apprenticeships and family help, and adopts tools once proven.
He goes from uneasy to **alarmed** with AGI in two years, and back to uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Hana's job and his post at risk while his **parents** depend on him.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for people like Hana, not just online courses.
Keeping **hands-on** clinical work with doctors by law.
